cross.generativity: Yes, strongly. All five converged on the same core: an op table with arity and defaults, canonical sorted-key arguments with -0 folded, SHA-256 over op + args + input ids, one frozen NodeRef per id, a separate result map keyed by id plus scale, and a copy on return. A, B, D and E also share a flat inputs-first closure with {id, op, inputs, args} and a domain/version tag in the hash. They differ in detail: B makes the walks iterative and the import atomic with id verification; A adds a cycle-detecting root-driven adopt; D verifies canonical bytes on a hit; E separates the argument registry from a pixel-function table. C departs: per-op objects merge registry and executor, the hash is delimiter-based and truncated, and the export is a nested tree.
cross.worse_is_better: Not here. C is the smallest (468 src lines) and its per-op co-location makes adding crop the most local, but it lost quality the bigger ones kept: unknown arguments are accepted, scale > 1 is accepted, the hash is truncated and not length-prefixed, and the nested export blows up on diamonds. Among the full-quality designs, A (585 lines) reaches nearly B's quality with less machinery. The chapter's extras that cost code without paying back (D's collision check on SHA-256, export versions that A and E never read) suggest the yardstick asks slightly too much in its implementation notes, not in its core.

Co-locate each op's normalisation and computation in one object so a new op is one edit (impl-C/src/index.ts:152-158, :202-313)

Derive the PRNG state by hashing the canonical seed so any numeric seed maps deterministically and -0 equals 0 (impl-B/src/index.ts:236-238, impl-D/src/index.ts:250, impl-E/src/index.ts:243)
